items.prompt: In the MediatR pipeline, AuthorizationBehaviour is registered before ValidationBehaviour. What does that ordering protect?
items.answer: Anonymous callers never get validation feedback that could leak which resources exist
distractors: Validation errors get logged together with the authenticated user's name
Validators can safely assume the request's IDs already belong to the caller
Performance timing then excludes the cost of the authorization database lookups
items.explanation: The ADR calls the order load-bearing: exception logging wraps authorization, authorization precedes validation, and performance timing is innermost so it measures only the handler.

items.prompt: Why are cross-cutting concerns implemented as MediatR behaviours rather than ASP.NET Core MVC filters or middleware?
items.answer: They must also apply to non-HTTP entry points, such as tests sending through ISender
distractors: MVC filters cannot read the request body, so FluentValidation could not run there
Middleware runs after the handler has finished, which is too late to stop a bad request
Behaviours are faster because they skip model binding and the routing middleware
items.explanation: The functional test that denies an anonymous user proves authorization works with zero HTTP involved - only possible because it is a behaviour.

items.prompt: PerformanceBehaviour is the innermost behaviour. What does its 500 ms warning therefore measure?
items.answer: Only the handler itself
distractors: The whole HTTP request, including model binding
Authorization plus validation, but not the handler
Only the time spent inside the EF interceptors
items.explanation: Being innermost, its stopwatch wraps only next() into the handler.

items.prompt: Which hidden cost does the behaviour pipeline add to every authenticated request?
items.answer: A database lookup of the username for log labels in two behaviours
distractors: Every request is validated twice, once on each pass through the pipeline
Each behaviour opens and commits its own DbContext transaction
The pipeline serialises requests, so only one handler can run at a time
items.explanation: The ADR lists I/O in the pipeline as a negative consequence, alongside hidden coupling.

items.prompt: A request carries [Authorize(Roles="A")] and [Authorize(Roles="B")]; the user is only in role B. What does AuthorizationBehaviour decide?
items.answer: Authorized: one flag spans all attributes, so they OR together
distractors: Forbidden: every attribute must be satisfied, as in ASP.NET Core itself
Forbidden: only the first [Authorize] attribute is ever evaluated
An exception, because two role attributes on one request are rejected at startup
items.explanation: The role loop sets authorized=true on any match across all attributes - a subtle divergence from ASP.NET Core's AND semantics.

items.prompt: Every TodoList endpoint requires authentication. What can an authenticated user still do, and why?
items.answer: Read or change other users' lists, because nothing records or checks an owner
distractors: Nothing harmful, because RequireAuthorization scopes every query to the caller
Only read other lists, because write commands are filtered by the CreatedBy column
Only see list titles, because the items are loaded through a per-user global filter
items.explanation: Authorization answers 'authenticated?' and 'in role?', never 'is this yours?'. Broken object-level authorization is OWASP API Top 10 #1.

items.prompt: A client sends colour "#BADBAD". What status does it get, and why?
items.answer: 500, because the domain exception is not mapped like validation failures
distractors: 400 ValidationProblemDetails, the same as any other invalid field
422, because the domain rejects the value after validation passes
200, because the colour is silently replaced with the default palette entry
items.explanation: Domain invariant violations and validation failures produce different contracts. The guide's preferred fix is both a validator rule and an exception mapping.

items.prompt: Which validation layer does the guide call the contract authority, and what is its weakness for cross-row rules such as a unique list title?
items.answer: FluentValidation in the pipeline; its uniqueness check races because nothing locks
distractors: Model binding; it cannot see the database, so uniqueness can never be checked there
Domain invariants; they only throw after SaveChanges has already written the row
UI hints; a maxLength attribute is trivially bypassed with curl or Postman
items.explanation: Validators aggregate every rule and can run async DB checks, but a check-then-insert across rows has no lock.

items.prompt: When does TodoItem raise TodoItemCompletedEvent?
items.answer: Only when Done changes from false to true, inside the setter
distractors: Every time Done is assigned true, even if it was already true
When the handler calls Publish after SaveChanges has succeeded
Whenever any property of an already completed item is changed
items.explanation: The invariant lives in the setter, so events fire correctly from every path, including seeds and tests.

items.prompt: Domain events are published by a SaveChanges interceptor before the commit. A handler sends an email, then the save fails. What happened?
items.answer: A ghost notification: the email left even though the change never committed
distractors: Nothing: the email is queued in the same transaction and rolled back
The save is retried until it succeeds, so the email becomes true
The interceptor publishes again after the retry, sending two emails
items.explanation: Pre-commit dispatch means external side effects escape the transaction; a handler throwing would instead abort the user's save.

items.prompt: What is the main benefit the authors bought by dispatching domain events before commit?
items.answer: Handlers writing to the same DbContext commit atomically with the trigger
distractors: Events survive a process crash, because they are persisted before dispatch
Handlers run on a background thread, off the user's HTTP request
External side effects such as emails are delivered exactly once
items.explanation: No dual-write for the in-DB case. The alternative, after-commit dispatch, inverts the failure mode: save succeeds, handler fails, event lost.

items.prompt: On the synchronous SavingChanges path, the interceptor calls DispatchDomainEvents(...).GetAwaiter().GetResult(). Why is that called a landmine?
items.answer: It blocks on async work, which deadlocks wherever a synchronization context exists
distractors: It swallows every exception thrown by the domain event handlers
It dispatches each event twice, once per SaveChanges overload
It moves the save onto a new thread-pool thread, which breaks the transaction
items.explanation: Sync-over-async deadlocks when the awaited continuation needs the context the caller is blocking.

items.prompt: When should this codebase move from in-process events to a transactional outbox?
items.answer: As soon as a handler performs external I/O such as sending email
distractors: Never: in-process dispatch already guarantees at-least-once delivery
Only once an event has more than one handler registered for it
As soon as the database provider moves from SQLite to SQL Server
items.explanation: Today every handler only logs, so the ghost-notification risk is latent; the outbox is the standard answer for reliable external side effects.

items.front: Name the two authorization enforcement points in netcleanarch and what each buys.
items.back: Endpoint groups with RequireAuthorization(): fail fast with a proper HTTP 401 challenge. [Authorize] on request records enforced by AuthorizationBehaviour: works without HTTP and survives new transports. Inconsistency: only GetTodosQuery carries [Authorize].

items.front: What does a senior check, in order, to rule out IDOR in a CRUD codebase?
items.back: 1) Does the resource have an owner/tenant column? 2) Is every read filtered by it? 3) Does every write verify it before mutating? 4) Is the check centralized (global query filter / policy) or copy-pasted? 5) Do tests prove cross-user denial?

items.front: Cookie vs bearer auth: which attack each shifts onto you, and when each fits.
items.back: Cookie: HttpOnly so XSS cannot read it, but sent automatically so CSRF becomes your problem; fits an SPA served by the API. Bearer: sent explicitly so CSRF is mostly moot, but client storage makes XSS your problem; fits public APIs, cross-origin and mobile.

items.front: Why does ADR-009 call these domain events 'synchronous method calls in disguise', and what delivery guarantee do they have?
items.back: Publish awaits all handlers inline, so their latency and failures land on the user's request. Delivery is at-most-once, in-process, and lost on crash.

items.prompt: A developer renames the endpoint handler method `GetTodoLists` to `FetchAllTodoLists`. According to the API-design guide, why is that a breaking API change?
items.answer: The operationId comes from the method name, so both SPAs get a renamed client method
distractors: The backend stops compiling, as a test project still calls the handler by its old name
Only server log labels change, as no client depends on any handler method name
Nothing visible changes, as NSwag names client methods from the route and verb
items.explanation: API design, Decision 1 (lines 15-19): the endpoint's name, which becomes the OpenAPI operationId, is derived from the handler method's name via `.WithName(handler.Method.Name)`, so the C# method GetTodoLists becomes the generated TypeScript method getTodoLists(). Renaming the method changes the operationId and therefore the generated client method in both SPAs, breaking every call site and any external OpenAPI consumer. In the incident (line 52) the backend CI stayed green because C# compiled fine; it was the frontend build that failed.

items.prompt: The API-design guide considered spelling every operationId out by hand, e.g. `.WithName("GetTodoLists")`, and rejected it as the default. What reason does it give?
items.answer: Renames tend to leave the literal stale, so code and contract silently disagree
distractors: NSwag ignores literal names, so the generated clients would lose those methods
Literal names cost a reflection lookup per request, which slows every endpoint
Pinned ids suit internal APIs only, and this API feeds external consumers too
items.explanation: Line 17: explicit operation IDs decouple the wire contract from the C# identifier, but they are boilerplate that drifts: people forget to update the string when they rename the method, and then code and contract disagree silently. Deriving the name from the method keeps them in lockstep by construction. The guide raises no NSwag or performance limitation, and line 19 says that for a public-facing API the author would pin explicit IDs, the opposite of reserving them for internal APIs.

items.prompt: A pull request adds a field to a command that clients must never be allowed to set. Per Decision 2 of the API-design guide, what should change?
items.answer: Give that endpoint a real request DTO and keep direct binding for the others
distractors: Put a request DTO and a mapper in front of every command across the whole API
Keep binding the command and add a validator rule that rejects the new field
Keep binding the command, as over-posting stays theoretical for record types
items.explanation: Line 27: commands are the bind target, so a client could set a server-controlled field in the request body (mass-assignment / over-posting), which the guide calls a real vulnerability, not a theoretical one, with nothing structural stopping it. Its prescription is to ask of each new field whether the client should be allowed to set it and, if not, to give that endpoint a real request DTO; the direct-bind convention is kept everywhere else, and a validator rule is not what the guide prescribes.

items.prompt: `UpdateTodoItem` returns BadRequest when the route id and the body id differ. Why does the API-design guide keep that check in the endpoint, and what risk does the author watch for?
items.answer: It is transport logic about URL versus body, and endpoints may accrete more logic
distractors: It is a business rule the handler lacks, and retries may skip the endpoint copy
It is transport logic about URL versus body, and a 404 may leak which ids exist
It needs the signed-in user's id, and it may end up running before authorization
items.explanation: Lines 38-40: the check is about the relationship between the URL and the payload, a transport-level HTTP idea the handler shouldn't need to know exists, so it stays in the endpoint. The tradeoff the author watches 'like a hawk' is growth: next a null check, then a 'quick' business rule, until endpoints hold logic the handlers don't know about and the tests don't cover. The guide classifies it as transport logic, not a business rule, and ties it to neither authentication nor resource-existence leaks.

items.prompt: The testing-strategy guide gives one rule for deciding which of its four test layers a new test belongs in. What is the rule?
items.answer: Use the lowest layer that can still observe the failure you actually fear
distractors: Use the highest layer so the test sees the failure through the full real stack
Use the fastest layer so the suite stays quick enough to run on each commit
Use each layer at once so every blind spot is covered by some other layer
items.explanation: Line 14: each layer's blind spot is another layer's target, and when you decide where a test goes the rule is to test at the lowest layer that can observe the failure you actually fear. Pushing a fear down a layer is faster but fictional; pushing it up is real but slow and vague. So the rule is neither 'highest' nor 'fastest', and it places a fear at one layer rather than at all of them.

items.prompt: Before the real-database functional suite existed, a handler used a LINQ filter the EF provider could not translate. Per the testing guide's incident, how did the problem first show up?
items.answer: As a production latency alarm, after the in-memory double had passed the tests
distractors: As a CI failure, after the in-memory provider rejected the untranslatable LINQ
As a constraint violation, after the mock enforced an index the database lacked
As a code review comment, after the reviewer flagged the client-side evaluation
items.explanation: Line 59: against the in-memory test double the expression evaluated client-side and passed every test; in production it threw a translation exception or, on an older EF version, silently pulled the whole table into memory. 'The first sign was a latency alarm, not a test failure, because the tests couldn't see it.' Line 22 adds that in-memory or mocked contexts accept queries the real provider can't translate and ignore constraints.

items.prompt: Two functional tests occasionally corrupt each other's data, and a colleague proposes marking them `[Parallelizable]` to shake out the flake. What does the testing guide say that would do, and what is the right first fix?
items.answer: It would cause the cross-talk, so first remove the static user fields in TestApp
distractors: It would be safe, as the static user fields are scoped to each test's own thread
It would speed things up safely, as Respawn already isolates each test's data
It would cause the cross-talk, so first give each test its own database copy
items.explanation: Lines 35-39: the test's current user is stored in static, process-global fields in TestApp, so two tests running at once would stomp on each other's identity, and Respawn's per-test reset assumes one test touches the database at a time; that is why the suite runs serially. Enabling parallelism would cause the very cross-talk the colleague imagines fixing, and the guide says the right fix is to remove the statics first.

items.prompt: Someone breaks the id-consistency check in `TodoItems.cs`, so a PUT with mismatched ids slips through. Per the testing guide, what happens in the test suites today?
items.answer: Both suites miss it, as functional tests enter below it and Todo.feature is missing
distractors: Application.FunctionalTests catch it, as they drive the PUT through routing and handlers
Web.AcceptanceTests catch it, as their Playwright features cover each todo screen
Domain.UnitTests catch it, as the id rule and its guard live in the TodoItem entity
items.explanation: Line 45: functional tests enter at ISender, below the endpoints, so endpoint code (the id-consistency guard, the status-code mapping, the model binding) is not covered by them, and the acceptance layer only covers Home/Counter/Weather/Login with no Todo.feature. The todo endpoints' HTTP behaviour is tested by neither suite; line 47 says breaking the check leaves every test green. The check lives in the endpoint, not in a domain entity.

items.prompt: A create request arrives with three invalid fields. What does the client get back, according to the error-handling guide?
items.answer: One 400 listing all three, gathered by the validation behaviour before one throw
distractors: One 400 naming the first failure, as validation halts at the first broken rule
One 400 listing all three, gathered by the endpoint from model-binding errors
One 400 per failing field, each sent as its own validator finishes in parallel
items.explanation: Line 14: ValidationBehaviour, a MediatR pipeline stage, runs all validators for the request, aggregates all failures and throws a single ValidationException carrying a PropertyName to messages dictionary, so the client gets every problem with its input at once. The aggregation happens in the pipeline behaviour, not in the endpoint, and line 52 describes one-failure-per-round-trip as exactly what this design prevented.

items.prompt: A fork's dashboard fired 500-rate alerts because an API integration sent unsupported colour codes. What standing practice does the error-handling guide draw from that incident?
items.answer: Grep Domain and Application for every Exception subclass and confirm it is mapped
distractors: Add a catch-all switch arm and report any unknown exception as a 400 instead
Route all API clients through the UI swatch picker so bad colours cannot arrive
Swap domain exceptions for Result objects so that none can escape a handler
items.explanation: Line 50: every exception type that can escape a handler needs a deliberate HTTP identity, so periodically grep the Domain and Application layers for `: Exception` and check each one is mapped; an unmapped domain exception is a latent 500. Line 28 keeps unmapped-to-500 as the right default for genuinely unexpected exceptions such as a NullReferenceException; the guide treats the API, not the UI, as the contract, and keeps throwing for domain-contract violations.

items.prompt: `IIdentityService.CreateUserAsync` returns a `Result`, while `UpdateTodoItem` throws `NotFoundException`. What does the error-handling guide say decides which mechanism a failure uses?
items.answer: Whether it is an expected outcome the caller branches on or an exceptional one
distractors: Whether it starts inside Identity library code or inside the app's own handlers
Whether it must reach the client as a 4xx status or may surface as a plain 500
Whether it was written before or after the team made Result the house default
items.explanation: Line 24: the codebase deliberately uses both. 'The password was too weak' is an expected outcome the caller branches on, so Identity returns a Result; domain-contract violations throw. The mature answer is that it depends on whether the failure is exceptional or expected. Line 22 says Result was rejected as the default, and the guide never chooses by where the code lives or by which status results.

items.prompt: A fork writes `[Authorize(Roles = "Admin, User")]`, with a space after the comma. Per the error-handling guide, what happens to a signed-in user whose only role is `User`?
items.answer: A 403, as splitting without Trim leaves a role named " User" that never matches
distractors: Access granted, as each split entry is trimmed before it meets the user's roles
A 401, as a role that can never match is treated like having no signed-in user
A startup failure, as role strings with spaces are refused at app registration
items.explanation: Line 38: the role check splits with `Split(',')` and no `Trim()`, so the second entry is a role literally named " User" that never matches. Line 36: UnauthorizedAccessException (401) is for no authenticated user at all, ForbiddenAccessException (403, line 11) for an authenticated user lacking the role, which is this user. The guide calls the edge latent because no caller passes such a string, so nothing rejects it at startup.

items.prompt: ADR-008 lists three rejected ways to run and isolate the functional tests. Why was transaction-rollback-per-test rejected?
items.answer: It breaks once a handler commits its own transaction, which every handler does
distractors: It is much slower than Respawn, as each test would boot its own database container
It relies on the in-memory provider, which accepts queries the real one cannot run
It clashes with the static current-user fields, which live outside any transaction
items.explanation: ADR-008 line 17: rollback-per-test breaks the moment code under test commits its own transaction, which every handler does. The other reasons belong to other choices: the mocked or in-memory context was rejected for passing queries the real provider can't translate (line 15), container-per-test for being far slower (line 16), and the static current-user fields are why the suite cannot run in parallel (line 27).

items.prompt: ADR-010 notes that `Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs` L33 suppresses EF Core's pending-model-changes warning. What consequence does the ADR attach to that?
items.answer: Schema drift goes unseen, as the alarm that the model diverged has been silenced
distractors: Seeding stops being idempotent, as each run re-inserts the sample todo lists
Migrations apply silently, as a destructive change can ship with no review step
Provider switches break, as only SQLite tolerates a pending model change on startup
items.explanation: ADR-010 line 28: schema drift is invisible because the pending-changes warning is suppressed; the exact alarm that would tell you the model diverged from a would-be migration is turned off. Line 11 says seeding is guarded so it is idempotent and that there is no migrations folder at all, and line 22 says one model targets three providers behind switches.

items.front: Name netcleanarch's four test projects, the seam each one enters at, and the real infrastructure each runs against.
items.back: Domain.UnitTests: plain objects, no infrastructure. Application.UnitTests: one class plus mocks, no infrastructure. Application.FunctionalTests: ISender, against a real database (Aspire + Respawn). Web.AcceptanceTests: a real browser (Playwright + Gherkin) over the full stack, SPA included.

items.front: What does the `AssertConfigurationIsValid()` test in MappingTests buy the team?
items.back: It turns 'we forgot to update the AutoMapper profile' from a runtime surprise into a build failure. One test, and the testing guide's author calls it their favorite in the repo.

items.front: Which HTTP status does ProblemDetailsExceptionHandler give a validation, a not-found, an unauthorized and a forbidden exception?
items.back: ValidationException: 400, with the field-errors dictionary as ValidationProblemDetails. NotFoundException (thrown by Guard.Against.NotFound): 404. UnauthorizedAccessException: 401. ForbiddenAccessException: 403. The last two are both thrown by AuthorizationBehaviour.

items.front: With one system-design or deep-dive interview slot, which ADR answers does the interview-translation guide say to lead with, and what should each one show?
items.back: ADR-003, ADR-009 or ADR-010. Each shows the junior-to-senior gradient in one breath: name the decision, what it costs, the failure mode, and the fix. The golden rule throughout: answer with a concrete example, a tradeoff and a failure mode, never a definition.

items.front: ADR-004: how do handlers reach EF Core, why is there no repository layer, and how does that tie into the testing strategy?
items.back: Application defines IApplicationDbContext (DbSet<TodoList>, DbSet<TodoItem>, SaveChangesAsync); ApplicationDbContext in Infrastructure implements it, and handlers use full LINQ against it. Repositories were rejected because they hide the EF coupling instead of removing it. The cost: handlers cannot be unit-tested against a mocked repository, so they need a real database, which is why ADR-008's testing strategy exists. The two decisions reinforce each other.

items.front: Why does the API-design guide treat netcleanarch's OpenAPI document as a build input rather than documentation?
items.back: Both frontends generate their typed API clients from it with NSwag (see ClientApp-React/nswag.json). The API is not the last stop: its contract feeds the builds of two other codebases.

items.front: How does an IEndpointGroup class become a live route group, and which C# language feature does the interface rely on?
items.back: At startup MapEndpoints reflects over the assembly and registers each class implementing IEndpointGroup as a route group named /api/{ClassName}, with a matching OpenAPI tag. The interface declares a `static abstract Map`, which was impossible before C# 11.
